newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian inflation seen under control-IBSA.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian inflation seen under control-IBSA.

text.p: Australian economists are optimistic on the outlook for inflation, and see interest rates on hold for much of 1997, according to a survey by the International Banks and Securities Association (IBSA).

"IBSA's economists' survey for March suggests that inflation is under control and that the outlook for the domestic economy is favourable, but there is still uncertainty in the currency and share markets, partly reflecting the international environment," ISBA executive director Robert Webster said.

"Underlying inflation will remain around two percent in 1997 but the headline CPI could be close to zero in the first half of the year as lower mortgage rates take effect," Macquarie Bank chief economist Bill Shields said.
With a favourable inflation outlook, there is little need seen for an interest rate hike in the near term.

"The Reserve Bank is likely to leave policy unchanged for the remainder of 1997 as the recovery in the domestic economy is unlikely to be sufficiently robust to raise concerns about inflation down the track," Schroders Australia senior economist Warren Tease said.

Last week, Reserve Bank Governor Ian Macfarlane said he saw underlying inflation remaining at around current levels for the forseeable future, and described the economy as free from major macroeconomic imbalances.

For inflation, economists remain optimistic and see wages as the only threat to continued good performance. In the year to December, underlying inflation rose 2.1 percent while the consumer price index (CPI) rose 1.5 percent.
Some, such as Dresdner Australia chief economist Rob Henderson, saw a possibility of a fourth quarter hike if the growth rebound turned into a boom.
Economists also said that the recent rise in Australian bond yields, with 10-year bond yields now above 8.0 percent, was overdone given current economic fundamentals.
Tease felt that bond yields may peak in the next month or so, before falling as the market reassessed Australia's inflation outlook.

While there was general agreement on the outlook for continued low inflation, economists were divided on the direction of the Australian dollar, with forecasts on a six month horizon ranging from US$0.74 to US$0.82.

Some saw expectations of stronger world growth, and therefore stronger commodity prices, supporting the dollar, although if the U.S. Federal Reserve were to tighten rates the dollar may experience some short term weakness.

Not all agreed. Rothschild Australia chief economist Ric Simes said "the Australian dollar appears to be stronger than warranted by fundamentals, and Tokai Australia economist Yasushi Usuda also expected a fall in the exchange rate, based on an anticipated rise in U.S. interest rates.
The U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meets on Tuesday this week and is widely expected to lift rates by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent.
On the outlook for the share market, there was a perception that a U.S. correction could outweigh sound local fundamentals.

Schroders' Tease said while domestic fundamentals such as profit growth and cost pressures would be positive for the equity market, "perceptions of a potential decline in U.S. share prices will weigh on Australian markets in the short term".
A U.S. rate hike could see further losses on Wall Street, but economists were not expecting a market collapse.
"There's a downward leg out there somewhere, given the near certainty of a U.S. correction," Bankers Trust Australia chief economist Chris Caton said.
"But a repeat of 1987 is not on the cards, and the Australian market is fundamentally good value," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
